title: Rutherford's Atomic Model and its Limitations
topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### 1. Meaning of the experiment

Thomson's plum-pudding model (1904) treated the atom as diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded in it and could not explain large-angle deflection of fast α-particles (He²⁺, ≈5.5 MeV). Rutherford with Geiger and Marsden (1909–1911) probed atomic *structure* by α-scattering — the experiment that established the **nuclear atom**.
### 2. Set-up

Radium in a lead block with a collimator gives a narrow α-beam; the target is gold foil ≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick (≈1000 atoms) because gold beats very thin and has a heavy nucleus (Z = 79); a rotatable ZnS screen viewed through a microscope records each scintillation; the apparatus is evacuated.
### 3. Observations
• ≈99.86% of α-particles passed straight through — the atom is mostly empty space.
• ≈1 in 20 000 was deflected by more than 90°, and a very few bounced back (θ ≈ 180°).
• Scattering obeys N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2); large-angle scattering is rare but real.
### 4. Conclusions (nuclear model)
• Atom is neutral and largely empty; a tiny, heavy, positive **nucleus** carries almost all the mass.
• Nuclear radius ≈10⁻¹⁵ m against atomic radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m (1 : 100 000); nuclear volume ≈10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume, nuclear density ≈10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
• Electrons revolve in circular orbits, the Coulomb attraction of the nucleus giving the centripetal force.
• The positive charge is characteristic of the element — the origin of atomic number, later proved by Moseley (1913).
### 5. Quantitative results
• Distance of closest approach (KE → electrostatic PE): r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m for 5 MeV α on gold — an experimental upper limit on nuclear size.
• Rutherford scattering law N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) explains why back-scattering is the rarest event.
### 6. Applications
• Founded nuclear physics: led to the proton (1919) and neutron (1932) and to nuclear fission/reactor technology; Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy (RBS) still analyses thin films industrially.
• Underpins Moseley's law and the atomic-number basis of the modern periodic table, and is the classic example of deducing structure statistically (probability) instead of by direct observation.
### 7. Limitations (exam-critical)
1. **Stability not explained:** a revolving electron is continuously accelerated, so by Maxwell's theory it must radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻⁸ s — yet atoms are stable.
2. **Line spectra not explained:** the inward spiral would emit a continuous range of frequencies, while hydrogen gives sharp discrete lines.
3. **No electronic arrangement:** nothing about shells, electron numbers or energies, so periodicity and valency remain unexplained.
4. **Purely classical:** circular orbits and a point nucleus are assumptions; without quantisation the model gives no orbital radii or energies.
5. **Ignores the neutron** (so isotopes are unexplained) and neglects electron–electron repulsion, so it fails for multi-electron atoms; no account of bonding or Zeeman/Stark splitting.
### 8. Exam pointers
Observations + conclusions and the two main defects (stability, discrete spectra) are standard 4–5 mark NEB questions; numericals use r₀, nuclear radius/density and the atom : nucleus volume ratio.
confusion: ❌ The atom is 'totally empty'. ✅ It is mostly empty *space*, but ≈99.9% of the mass lies in the nucleus.
❌ α-particles are electrons. ✅ They are helium nuclei (+2e, ≈7300 times heavier than an electron), so electrons cannot deflect them appreciably.
❌ The model failed because α-particles were absorbed. ✅ Scattering itself was explained well; the model failed on stability and line spectra.
❌ Atom radius = nuclear radius. ✅ 10⁻¹⁰ m versus 10⁻¹⁵ m.

universalFacts: α-scattering experiment: 1909–1911; Geiger and Marsden counted ≈1 flash in 10⁴ at large angles; gold foil ≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick.
Rutherford received the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on radioactivity.
Nuclear density is nearly the same for all nuclei because R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.
examples: **Problem:** Find r₀ for a 5.0 MeV α-particle on gold (Z = 79). **Solution:** KE = 5.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J; r₀ = (2 × 9×10⁹ × 79 × (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²)/(8.0 × 10⁻¹³) ≈ 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Since r₀ is larger than the nuclear radius, the nucleus acts as a point charge and the α-particle is never captured.
importantNotes: Quote the radiating-electron instability (collapse in ≈10⁻⁸ s) and the continuous-versus-line-spectrum defect first.
Never claim Rutherford's model explained the hydrogen spectrum — repairing that was Bohr's achievement (1913).
summary: Rutherford's α-scattering work (1909–1911, with Geiger and Marsden) replaced Thomson's plum-pudding atom with the nuclear atom: a tiny, heavy, positively charged nucleus (r ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m, density ≈2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³) carrying nearly all the mass inside an atom that is otherwise empty space (r ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m), with electrons revolving around it under Coulomb attraction. The two quantitative results are the distance of closest approach, r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE), and the scattering law N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2). The model explains the observations superbly but fails fatally on two points — a revolving electron must radiate and spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻⁸ s, and it would emit a continuous spectrum instead of hydrogen's sharp lines — and it offers no electronic arrangement, which is why Bohr's quantised model became necessary in 1913.
importantConcepts: Nuclear model: a tiny heavy positive nucleus in a mostly empty atom, electrons revolving with Coulomb attraction as the centripetal force
α-scattering observations and inferences: ≈99.86% undeflected, 1 in 20 000 beyond 90°, very few back-scattered
Scattering law N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) and distance of closest approach r₀ = 2kZe²/KE
Size data: nuclear radius ≈10⁻¹⁵ m against atomic radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m, nuclear density ≈2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³
Limitations: radiating-electron instability, continuous-spectrum prediction, no electronic arrangement, classical assumptions, no neutron
importantStatements: The atom is mostly empty space, yet nearly 99.9% of its mass lies in the nucleus.
A classical revolving electron is accelerated, so it must radiate and spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻⁸ s — yet atoms are stable.
The inward spiral would emit a continuous range of frequencies, contradicting hydrogen's discrete line spectrum.
The nuclear radius (≈10⁻¹⁵ m) is about 1/100 000 of the atomic radius (≈10⁻¹⁰ m), so nuclear volume is ≈10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume.
The model gives no shells, energies or electronic arrangement, so periodicity and valency stay unexplained, and ignoring the neutron leaves isotopes unexplained.

keyPoints: Undeflected majority → empty space; large-angle scattering → concentrated charge; back-scattering → a very small nucleus.
r₀ ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m for a 5 MeV α-particle on gold — an experimental upper limit on nuclear size.
N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) explains why 180° scattering is the rarest event.
Defect 1: accelerated charge radiates → energy loss → spiral inward → no stable atoms.
Defect 2: the changing revolution frequency would give a continuous spectrum, not lines.
specialNotes: The atom is not 'totally empty' — it is mostly empty space, but almost all the mass is nuclear.
α-particles are helium nuclei (+2e), ≈7300 times heavier than an electron, so only the nucleus can deflect them.
The scattering itself was explained well: the model failed on stability and line spectra, not on the observations.
examShortTricks: List the limitations in this order: stability → line spectra → no electronic arrangement → classical assumptions → ignores the neutron.
Pair every observation with its conclusion; the marks are for the inference, not for listing the apparatus.
r₀ = 2kZe²/KE, and always follow the number with 'an upper limit on nuclear size'.
